title: Janabai at the grindstone
hookLine: a woman at a grinding stone before dawn, singing, and a story that says God sat down and turned the stone with her
carry: bhakti belongs to everyone, even at the grindstone
tomorrow: the line to Vitthal is hours long. was the whole walk wasted?
last: A TEACHER'S SANDALS CARRY THE TEACHER.

cards: It's still dark. A woman sits at a grinding stone, the heavy round kind turned by hand, and the grain goes in a little at a time. It's slow work, and to keep the rhythm she sings.
That's Janabai, remembered as a servant in Namdev's household.

The story Varkaris tell about her is that one morning, when the work was too much, Vitthal himself sat down beside her and took the handle, and the two of them turned the stone together while she sang.
Today, the songs of the road, and who was allowed to sing them.

teach.b: The songs the Varkaris sing on the road are called abhangs: short verses in Marathi, made to be sung with cymbals and a drum, in call and answer.
One voice leads, the dindi answers, and the line goes round and round until the whole group is carrying it. Now look at who made them. Jnaneshwar was born to a family the village had cast out.
Namdev was from a family of tailors. Tukaram kept a grocery.
And Janabai, by tradition, ground grain and carried water in someone else's house.
Her songs speak to Vitthal with startling closeness; some tell him he's late, some call him mother, and the grinding-stone story says he answered by working beside her. Then there's Chokhamela.
Tradition remembers him as a Mahar, from a community kept outside the temple, so he sang to Vitthal from beyond its walls.
Some of his songs ask, plainly, why the body others call impure should be shut out, when it holds the same God. His abhangs are still sung on the road.
So the songs that carry the walk were made, in good part, by people who could not have stood in front of a priest and been heard. On the road, their voices lead the singing.

That's the bhakti saints' teaching: love for God doesn't wait on birth or learning, and work done singing to God is worship. Janabai's grain counts. The week began with a cat in Bengal and ends at a grindstone.

how: Varkaris sing abhangs in call and answer, with cymbals and a drum, during the wari and at gatherings at home; the songs of Janabai and Chokhamela are among those sung.

games.q: you're Janabai, at the grinding stone before dawn. the work is too much, and the day's barely begun. what do you do?
o: stop and wait for someone to notice.
keep turning the stone, and keep singing to Vitthal.
games.why: she keeps working and singing, and the story says Vitthal sat down and turned the stone with her.

practice: Feel the rhythm of one plain, repeated job you do, washing dishes, folding laundry, typing, driving, and breathe in that rhythm slowly, as if the job were a song.
If a line of a song you love comes to you, let it hum quietly inside. If you pray, you can imagine, as Janabai's story does, that you aren't doing that job alone.

wordCard.voice: Maharashtra's Varkari. The tradition whose road songs were made by a servant at a grindstone, a tailor, a grocer, and a man kept outside the temple. Today's word.
